refusal.body: Help explains how the product works. It does not answer questions about a patient. Open the patient's page to see their results and where each one comes from.

articles.title: What Help can and cannot answer
body: Help explains how the product works: what a screen shows, what a word or a status means, and why a control may be unavailable to you or in this environment.
It does not answer questions about a patient. A patient's page shows their results, and each result shows where it comes from.

articles.title: What the home page shows
body: The home page is your worklist: what needs a person today. It lists the follow-ups assigned to you and the results that are held, each line opening the patient's page where the work is done.
The list is in a fixed order. It does not rank anything by clinical urgency, and an empty section only says that nothing is listed there.

articles.title: What a held result means
body: A result is held when the product could not produce guidance from a report, for example because the report's findings have not been reviewed yet or a needed gene result is missing.
A held result shows no guidance. Its line says why it is held and what a reviewer can do about it. Holding is how the product avoids showing guidance it cannot back up.

articles.title: Follow-ups
body: A follow-up is a reminder to check on a patient's treatment later, for example some weeks after a medication is started. Each one has a date, a time zone and the person it is assigned to.
Overdue means the reminder date has passed. It does not say how urgent the patient's situation is. The Follow-ups page lists the clinic's follow-ups, with filters.

articles.title: Finding or adding a patient
body: Patients are identified by a synthetic label. Open Patients and type part of the label to find one. While more patients remain to load, choose Search all patients to look through every one.
A clinician can choose Add patient to create one. The label is recorded first, then the fictional demographics on the patient's page.

articles.title: Attaching a report
body: Choose Attach a report on the home page or on Reports. Choose the patient, then the file and its type, confirm that the file holds synthetic data only, then choose Upload report. If a reload interrupts an upload, the same page offers to finish or cancel it.
The Reports page lists every report and whether its file was verified. Verifying a file confirms that it was stored unchanged. It does not check what the report says.

articles.title: The genomic profile
body: A patient's page shows their genomic profile: each gene from their accepted reports, with its phenotype and the report it came from, and their current medications checked against the guidelines loaded in the product.

Each medication shows the guideline's own wording. Why, and the evidence opens where that wording comes from. When two reports disagree about a gene, both are shown and the product does not choose between them.

articles.title: When another medication can change a gene's effect
body: Another medication can change how well a gene's protein works, so a person can respond differently from what their genes predict. This is called phenoconversion.

When a current medication is listed by the FDA as a strong or moderate inhibitor or inducer of a gene that guidance relies on, the patient's page says so beside that guidance. The guidance itself is still based on the genes alone.
The FDA list is not complete, and stopped medications are not checked.

articles.title: Recording a decision
body: A clinician records a decision on a result: accepted, modified, rejected, deferred or clarification requested, with a note in their own words.

Decisions can be switched off in an environment. The page then says that decisions are not switched on in this environment and offers no form. That is a setting of the environment, not something about the patient.

articles.title: What each role can do
body: A reader reads patient records and results. A clinician can also add patients, attach reports and record medications, decisions and follow-ups. A reviewer reads records and does the reviews that need a second person.
An administrator manages the organization's members and sees its usage, but nothing clinical. A control your role cannot use is not shown to you.

articles.title: Synthetic data only
body: Everything in this product is synthetic: invented patients, invented reports and test settings. It is not approved for clinical use.
Do not enter real patient information anywhere in it.

articles.title: The words used on the screens
body: Words such as phenotype, diplotype and poor metabolizer have short explanations. On a patient's page, a word with an explanation is a button: select it to read what it means, and Words used here lists them all.
Each explanation says whether a pharmacist has reviewed it yet.

articles.title: Where the policies are
body: The product's policies, its privacy policy included, have not been published yet. Help will point to them here once they are.
